meta.title: Who really said "What is now proved was once only imagined"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it is genuine William Blake, from “The Marriage of Heaven and Hell” (Proverbs of Hell, plate 8, c. 1790). The original reads ‘once, only imagin’d.’
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What is now proved was once only imagined'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Blake — from The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Proverbs of Hell, plate 8 (c. 1790). Original: 'once, only imagin'd.'

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From “The Marriage of Heaven and Hell” (composed c. 1790), in the “Proverbs of Hell” on plate 8. Blake’s own engraved text reads “What is now proved was once, only imagin’d” — the familiar modern wording simply regularizes the spelling and drops the comma.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell

source.excerpt:
The eagle never lost so much time, as when he submitted to learn of the crow.

What is now proved was once, only imagin’d.

The rat, the mouse, the fox, the rabbet: watch the roots; the lion, the tyger, the horse, the elephant, watch the fruits.
trail: The line sits among the aphoristic “Proverbs of Hell” on plate 8 — confirmed in the Wikisource text ↗.
Blake’s engraved wording is “What is now proved was once, only imagin’d” — per the Erdman edition of Blake’s Complete Poetry and Prose ↗.
“The Marriage of Heaven and Hell” was composed and printed by Blake around 1790 — see the William Blake Archive ↗.
source.excerptNote: As engraved by Blake on plate 8 of “The Marriage of Heaven and Hell.” Spelling and punctuation are Blake’s own.

author.name: William Blake
author.heading: About William Blake
author.bio: William Blake (1757–1827) was an English poet, painter and engraver, now regarded as a seminal figure of the Romantic age though largely unrecognized in his lifetime. He produced his major prophetic works as “illuminated books,” etching text and image together and printing them by hand. The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (c. 1790), with its provocative “Proverbs of Hell,” is among his most quoted works.

misattribution.heading: A note on the wording
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Blake is correct — but the line is almost always quoted in a lightly modernized form.

items.why: Modern quotations read “What is now proved was once only imagined,” whereas Blake’s engraved plate reads “What is now proved was once, only imagin’d” — with a comma after “once” and the archaic spelling “imagin’d,” per the Erdman edition ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are genuinely Blake’s, from the “Proverbs of Hell” in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell ↗; only the spelling and punctuation have been smoothed over time.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The “Proverbs of Hell” are deliberately provocative aphorisms voiced from Blake’s infernal, energy-affirming perspective in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell. This line distills his lifelong conviction that imagination is not idle fancy but the seedbed of reality — that what is later demonstrated or built began as something merely conceived.
